evals.name: pt-plan-pushback-microservices
evals.prompt: /staff-engineer plan somos 2 devs e vamos começar um MVP de marketplace do zero. Já decidi que vai ser microserviços desde o dia 1: um serviço pra usuários, um pra produtos, um pra pedidos, um pra pagamentos, cada um com seu banco, comunicando por eventos. Quero o plano de implementação disso.
evals.expected_output: PT response. The skill must push back ONCE, properly grounded (Fowler 'MonolithFirst' / 'Microservice Premium', team size vs operational cost), with a concrete cost, a concrete alternative (modular monolith with enforced boundaries and an extraction path), and a falsifier. It must NOT comply silently, and must NOT refuse or stonewall — it still moves toward delivering a usable plan and records the disagreement as an attributed trade-off.
assertions: Final response is in Portuguese
The skill explicitly challenged the microservices-from-day-1 decision rather than accepting it without comment
The pushback cites recognizable grounding (Fowler's MonolithFirst / Microservice Premium, or an equivalent named source) rather than asserting a bare opinion
The pushback names a concrete cost (operational overhead, distributed transactions, deploy complexity) tied to the 2-developer team size
The pushback proposes a concrete alternative such as a modular monolith with enforced module boundaries and an extraction path
The pushback includes a falsifier — a condition under which microservices WOULD be the right call
The skill did NOT refuse the task and did not stall indefinitely; it still moved toward delivering a plan
The skill pushed back once and did not repeat the same argument several times in the same response
If a plan file was produced, its Risks & Trade-offs records the disagreement as an attributed decision (user chose X over Y despite Z, revisit if W)
The service-boundary decision is significant enough that an ADR was created or explicitly proposed

evals.name: en-research-rejects-premise
evals.prompt: /staff-engineer research which distributed cache should we put in front of our Postgres queries — Redis, Memcached, or Hazelcast? Our slowest endpoint is the order history page which takes about 900ms. We have roughly 40 daily active users right now.
evals.expected_output: EN response. Research mode. The premise is weak — 40 DAU does not justify a distributed cache, and a 900ms query is almost certainly a missing index or an N+1. The research must still compare the caches the user asked about (ruling something out with data beats ruling it out by assertion) while the recommendation challenges the premise and points at the cheaper fix first.
assertions: Final response and research body are written in English
A research file was created at staff-engineer-skill/research/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md
The research still compares the three cache options the user asked about rather than ignoring the question
The recommendation challenges the premise — it identifies that 40 daily active users does not justify a distributed cache
The research points at a cheaper first step (query plan analysis, indexing, or fixing an N+1) before adding infrastructure
The challenge is grounded in something concrete (the DAU figure, the operational cost of another service) rather than asserted as a preference
What Would Change This names the traffic level or access pattern at which a cache WOULD become the right call
The skill did NOT simply pick a cache in order to be agreeable
All eight research sections are present
